segments.text: Good morning. Today we move from estimation to hypothesis testing, which is the second half of inference.
segments.speaker: professor

segments.text: Last week we built confidence intervals. A test asks a sharper question: is the data compatible with one specific value?
segments.speaker: professor

segments.text: We always start from two statements. The null hypothesis, H zero, and the alternative, H one.
segments.speaker: professor

segments.text: The null is the boring claim. For example, the mean waiting time at the clinic is twenty minutes.
segments.speaker: professor

segments.text: The alternative is what we would believe if the evidence is strong enough. Say, the mean is longer than twenty minutes.
segments.speaker: professor

segments.text: Notice the asymmetry. We never prove the null. We either reject it, or we fail to reject it.
segments.speaker: professor

segments.text: Now, the test statistic. For a mean with known sigma, we use z equals x bar minus mu zero, over sigma divided by root n.
segments.speaker: professor

segments.text: Under the null, this statistic follows a standard normal distribution. That is the whole trick.
segments.speaker: professor

segments.text: Let us do the example on the slide. Sample of thirty-six patients, sample mean twenty-two point five minutes, sigma six.
segments.speaker: professor

segments.text: So z is two point five divided by one, which gives two point five.
segments.speaker: professor

segments.text: Is two point five large? We compare it with the critical value. At the five percent level, one-sided, the critical value is one point six four five.
segments.speaker: professor

segments.text: Two point five is beyond one point six four five, so we reject the null hypothesis at the five percent level.
segments.speaker: professor

segments.text: The p-value says the same thing in a different language. It is the probability, under the null, of a result at least this extreme.
segments.speaker: professor

segments.text: Here the p-value is about zero point zero zero six. Small p-value, strong evidence against the null.
segments.speaker: professor

segments.text: A very common mistake in the exam: the p-value is not the probability that the null is true. Please do not write that.
segments.speaker: professor

segments.text: Two kinds of error. Type one error: we reject a true null. Its probability is alpha, the significance level we choose.
segments.speaker: professor

segments.text: Type two error: we fail to reject a false null. Its probability is beta, and one minus beta is the power of the test.
segments.speaker: professor

segments.text: There is a trade-off. If you make alpha smaller, beta grows, unless you collect a larger sample.
segments.speaker: professor

segments.text: Two-sided tests split alpha in the two tails. At five percent, the critical values become plus and minus one point nine six.
segments.speaker: professor

segments.text: When sigma is unknown, we replace it with the sample standard deviation and use the t distribution with n minus one degrees of freedom.
segments.speaker: professor

segments.text: The logic does not change. Only the table you read the critical value from.
segments.speaker: professor

segments.text: For next week, do exercises four to nine in problem set four. Exercise seven is the kind of question I like for the exam.
segments.speaker: professor

segments.text: Any questions? Yes. Can we use the confidence interval to run the test? Good question, and yes, for a two-sided test they agree.
segments.speaker: professor

segments.text: If the hypothesized value falls outside the ninety-five percent interval, you reject at the five percent level. Same decision.
segments.speaker: professor
